title: Build three-point lighting, one light at a time
standards: MA MP-B Standard 5 (lighting, sets and props)
standardsNote: Standard-level tags only, from the brief. Tom will supply the exact codes.

steps.text: Three-point lighting uses three lights with three jobs: a key light, a fill light and a back light. You'll add them one at a time and watch what each one does to the picture.
Start with a dark studio: every light off, white paper behind the subject.
Add a key light. Under the map, pick a light (try the Neewer CB60 RGB), set its job to Key light, and press + Add light. Then drag it to about 45° camera-left, a little above the face.
steps.hint: The K marker should sit to the left of the subject on the map, between the subject and the camera.
steps.success: Look at the face: one side lit, one side in shadow.

steps.question: With only the key light on, what does the side of the face away from the key look like?
options: Just as bright as the key side
The same colour as the backdrop
steps.explain: The key light sets the direction of the shadows. With nothing else lighting it, the far side falls into shadow.

steps.question: Now a fill light goes on the other side of the camera, dimmer than the key. What will it do to the shadow side?
options: Lighten it, but leave it a little darker than the key side
steps.explain: A fill light softens the shadows the key makes without wiping them out. That leftover shadow is what gives the face shape.

steps.text: Adjust the fill so the shadow side is about half a stop to one and a half stops darker than the lit side. The description under the camera view tells you how many stops.
steps.hint: Lower the fill's power, or move it farther away, to deepen the shadows. Raise it or move it closer to lighten them.

steps.question: Last, a back light goes behind the subject, aimed at the back of the head. What will it add?
options: Light on the front of the face
A rim of light on the head and shoulders
steps.explain: The back light outlines the head and shoulders, which separates the subject from the backdrop.

steps.question: Which light sets the direction of the shadows?
steps.explain: The key is the main, brightest light, so its shadows are the ones you see.

steps.prompt: In two or three sentences, explain what each of the three lights did to the picture.
